1394.title: When the church does wrong
1394.hook: the church has harmed people; honesty, repentance and justice are required
1394.howItsDone: Christians practice repentance through confession, private or in a liturgy, and churches of several traditions have made public confessions and apologies, opened independent investigations, and offered redress to people harmed by church leaders or institutions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: miracles as signs, and Augustine's vineyards. Your line was every day a miracle.

Some hard words about the church are inside the Bible itself. A letter of Peter puts it flatly: "For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God." Not out there, with the outsiders. At the house of God. It matters, because churches have harmed people. Abuse, and abuse covered up. People shamed, driven out, told God was finished with them. Congregations that stood beside cruelty and called it order. Saying so out loud isn't an attack on faith. The Bible sets the pattern for it.
screen: `JUDGMENT BEGINS AT THE HOUSE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: In year three, the line was believe them. This lesson asks what comes next. The Bible's word is repent, and it gives three pictures of what that looks like when a whole community has gone wrong. First, honesty that says we. Daniel prays over the wrongs of his people. He doesn't point at them from a safe distance: "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled." He stands inside the failure instead of beside it. Second, a turned life. To people coming out to be baptized, John the Baptist says: "Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance." Fruit you can see. In Luke, when people ask what to do, his answers are concrete: share your coat, take no more than you're owed, don't bully anyone with your power. Repentance shows up in how you act on Monday. Third, repair. Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, and rich, meets Jesus, and in his own house he stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Not just sorry. Paid back, and more. Churches have tried to walk this road, some with public confessions, apologies, investigations and payments to survivors. Some have walked it well, some slowly, some not yet, and the people who were harmed are often the ones who can say how far it still has to go. In these texts, judgment begins at the house of God. So does repentance.

Bring to mind people who have been harmed by a church: someone you know, someone whose story you've read, maybe yourself, and let them be real to you without explaining their hurt away or rushing to defend anyone. If you pray, hold them before God, by name or in silence, and ask for truth, justice and healing; if you don't, hold them in mind with respect. If you're being harmed now, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
When the church does wrong. The Bible's answer is honest confession, a turned life and real repair, beginning at the house of God.
screen: `WHEN THE CHURCH DOES WRONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: repent. Zacchaeus didn't stop at sorry; he paid it back. See you tomorrow.

1395.title: Church hurt
1395.hook: many have been wounded by Christians; healing may take time and distance
1395.howItsDone: Some Christians who have been hurt in church step away for a season, find a different congregation, or work through it with a counselor or a trusted pastor; some churches run listening sessions or support for people who were harmed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: judgment begins at the house of God, and Zacchaeus paid it back fourfold. Your line was repent.

A woman drives past the church she grew up in. Same red door. Same sign out front with the sermon title in plastic letters. She hasn't been inside for years, and her stomach still tightens at the sight of it. Somebody in there once told her something about herself, and about God, that she's still trying to unhear. Friends ask when she'll go back, as if it were a cold she ought to be over. Some people carry wounds that came from Christians, in a place that was meant to be safe.

Year one met this with a bruised reed; today goes further. Ezekiel has a whole chapter on it. God speaks against the shepherds of Israel, the leaders meant to care for the people, and the charges are specific: "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken." Then the verdict: "with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them." The text doesn't scold the sheep for scattering. God says what he will do himself: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." Some sheep didn't wander off. They were pushed. Matthew borrows Isaiah's words to describe Jesus: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench." A reed already bent, a lamp wick barely smoking: care that goes slowly with damaged things. And the Teacher in Ecclesiastes, listing the seasons of a life, includes "a time to heal." Healing has its own season, and it isn't rushed. For some people healing means going back to church, sometimes a different one. For some it means a long season away. Some never go back. Some readers draw a gentle way of standing beside a hurt person from these texts: no rushing, no arguing them back, no turning their pain into a debate about defending the institution. Bind up, and let them set the pace.
screen: `A BRUISED REED SHALL HE NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Suppose a friend sits down across from you and says, a church hurt me, and notice the first thing you want to say: an explanation, a defense. Set it down like a heavy bag, and just listen; if the friend is you, listen to yourself the same way, and if you pray, ask that they be bound up gently, at their own pace. If the hurt included abuse, or ever feels too heavy, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Church hurt. Wounds that come from a church or from Christians. In Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away.
Your line: healing takes time. Ezekiel's God seeks the ones driven away. I'll be here tomorrow.

1396.title: We are all hypocrites
1396.hook: people often say the church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints
1396.howItsDone: Church services in several traditions include a general confession said together by the whole congregation, in which everyone, clergy included, admits their sin before God; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess privately to a priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, church hurt: in Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away. Your line was healing takes time.

"They're all hypocrites." It gets said about churches at family dinners, in comment sections, sometimes with anger and sometimes with a tired shrug. And there's a reply some Christians give that surprises people: yes. All of us. A saying gets passed around about it: the church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints. Nobody seems sure who said it first, and it isn't a Bible verse. But it points at something the Bible says plainly, and says first about its own people.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his own disciples about how they give and pray. Don't sound a trumpet when you give to the poor, he says. Don't pray on the street corners like the hypocrites, "that they may be seen of men." A hypocrite, in his picture, is someone performing goodness for an audience. Then comes an image that's almost a cartoon: "Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." A wooden beam sticking out of your face while you squint at the speck in someone else's. Some readers hear a joke in it, and then a wince. Paul doesn't claim to have it together. In Romans he writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." The gap between what he believes and what he does is a place he lives. And he widens the circle to include everyone: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." All. That's where all of us comes from. And Jesus said who he came for: "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." So when someone says the church is full of hypocrites, a Christian who has read these texts can agree without flinching. In its own scriptures, the church was never meant to be a gallery of finished people. The danger Jesus names isn't the struggle. It's the performance: pretending the beam isn't there.
screen: `SEEN OF MEN: GOODNESS AS A SHOW.`
`THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.`

segments.voice: Start with someone else's speck, a fault in another person that gets under your skin, then turn the question around: where does some version of that live in you, or what value do you talk about but don't live? Don't punish yourself; look at the beam plainly, the way you'd look at a splinter you finally want out. Name it honestly to yourself, and if you pray, name it to God.
We are all hypocrites. Not an excuse but an admission: Paul's all have sinned, said with the word we.
Your line: all of us. A hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints. Until tomorrow.

1397.title: Wounded healers
1397.hook: our wounds, healed, can help others
1397.howItsDone: Some Christians serve others through what they have suffered: in grief groups, recovery groups, hospital visiting and prison ministry, people who have walked through something offer their company to those who are walking through it now.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the beam in your own eye, and Paul's all have sinned. Your line was all of us.

A church basement on a weeknight. A steel coffee urn, a box of tissues passed hand to hand. The person who runs the group doesn't have a degree in anything. What she has is a memory: years ago she sat in that same room, shaking, and somebody who'd been there before her stayed until the end of the night. Now she's the one who stays. There's a name for people like her. Henri Nouwen, a Catholic priest and writer, used it as the title of a book.

Paul opens his second letter to Corinth praising God "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Read it slowly and it's a relay. The comfort you were handed is the comfort you hand on. And Paul isn't writing from a comfortable chair. A few lines later he says they were "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." The healer is still limping. Then Isaiah's servant song, met in year two, which Christians read about Jesus: "with his stripes we are healed." Stripes: the marks left by blows. Here, healing comes through wounds, not around them. Then Luke. The risen Jesus stands among his frightened friends, who think they are seeing a spirit, and he says, "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself." Luke doesn't describe the marks; John's Gospel does, with the print of the nails. But in Luke the hands and feet that went to the cross are how his friends know him. So a healed wound isn't one that never happened. It's one that closed and left a mark that can be shown. That doesn't mean every hurt has to be put to work right away. A wound that's still bleeding needs care first, and nobody owes anyone their story. But the ones that have closed can become a map for someone still lost in the same country.

Go back to one wound that has mostly healed, a loss, a failure, an illness, a hard year; not the one that's still raw, which can stay in care for now. Notice what got you through, a person, a sentence somebody said, a small kindness, and ask who is standing in that place now; if you pray, ask how your scar might help them. If an old wound ever opens into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Wounded healers. People whose healed hurts help them help others, the way Paul says comfort received becomes comfort given.
Your line: wounds that heal. Comfort received becomes comfort given. Go gently.

1398.title: Fear not
1398.hook: fear not appears again and again in scripture
1398.howItsDone: Christians often memorize fear-not verses such as Isaiah 41:10 and say them in anxious moments, and the angel's 'fear not' to the shepherds is read aloud in churches at Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wounded healers: comfort received becomes comfort given. Your line was wounds that heal.

Abram, in a vision, childless and waiting. A young woman in Nazareth, with an angel in the room. Shepherds in a dark field, suddenly lit up. Women at a tomb that should not be empty. John on the island of Patmos, falling at someone's feet as though dead. Different places, different stories, different people. And to each of them, heaven says the same two words. Fear not.

You heard it in year two, said to a little flock. Now listen to what comes right after those words. To Abram: "Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward." To Mary: "Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God." To the shepherds: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." To John on Patmos, with a right hand laid on him: "Fear not; I am the first and the last." And through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, called my servant: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God." Hear the pattern? For. I am. Behold. In these passages, fear not is never just a command left hanging. It's a sentence with a second half, and the second half is a reason, usually a presence. And the frightened people aren't scolded. Luke says the shepherds were "sore afraid." The angel doesn't tell them they're overreacting. It gives them news big enough to step out of the fear. Then notice when the words come. Abram is waiting on a promise. Mary is about to say yes to something enormous. The women at the tomb are standing at the edge of a story that's just changed. Fear not keeps showing up at thresholds, right before something new. So in scripture, fear not doesn't pretend fear isn't there. It speaks to the fear directly, and then it gives a reason.
screen: `FEAR NOT, ABRAM: I AM THY SHIELD.`

segments.voice: Let one fear come up, about money, your health, a person you love, what's coming next, and name it plainly without arguing with it. Then say the two words to it, out loud or inside, fear not, and give it a second half the way scripture does. If you pray, borrow Isaiah's, for I am with thee; if you don't, let the second half be something true and steady: I'm breathing, I'm here, this moment holds.
Fear not. Heaven's words to Abram, Mary, the shepherds and John, each time followed by a reason: I am, for, behold.
Your line: fear not. The shepherds were sore afraid, and nobody scolded them. See you in the morning.

1399.title: Cast your care (1 Peter 5:7)
1399.hook: cast all your care on him, for he cares for you
1399.howItsDone: Christians bring worries to God in private prayer, in prayer journals and on prayer lists, and some churches keep prayer boxes or prayer walls where people leave written requests; 1 Peter 5:7 is often memorized and said in anxious moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear not: heaven's word to Abram, Mary and the shepherds, each time with a second half. Your line was fear not.

A sticky note on the fridge, half hidden under a magnet: the dentist, the rent, the thing with your sister, the noise the car is making. Lists like that have a way of growing. Cross one thing off and two more appear. Near the end of a short letter from Peter, written to Christians going through suffering, there's one sentence aimed at that list. In the King James words: "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you."

Start with the verb. Cast is not set down politely. It's a throwing word. The same verb turns up in Luke, when the disciples throw their garments onto a colt for Jesus to ride. A physical motion: off you, onto something else. Peter ties it to the line just before: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." In this letter, handing over worry is a kind of humility. It's admitting you were never built to carry everything. The picture is older than Peter's letter. Psalm 55 says, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee." Notice the promise. Not that the burden disappears, but that you'll be held up. Sustained. Then a story that shows the throw happening. Hannah longs for a child and has none. At the sanctuary in Shiloh she prays so hard, lips moving and no sound, that the priest Eli thinks she's drunk. She tells him she has "poured out my soul before the LORD." Eli sends her off in peace. And then the text says: "the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." Nothing had changed yet. No child, no answer, no news. But she had thrown it, and she ate her dinner. Last, the reason at the end of Peter's sentence: for he careth for you. The care you throw lands with someone who cares about you. In English it's the same word, care, going both ways.

Take a scrap of paper or open a note on your phone, write one worry in a few plain words, and look at it for a moment. Then fold the paper and set it down out of reach, or close the note. If you pray, say the verse as you do it, casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you; if you don't, let the motion say: I don't have to hold this every second.
Cast your care. Throw your worry onto God, the letter of Peter says, because he cares for you.
Your line: he cares for you. Hannah threw it, and then she ate her dinner. That's today, done.

1400.title: Loneliness
1400.hook: God sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6)
1400.howItsDone: Christians care for lonely people through home visits, bringing communion to people who can't leave home, shared meals after services, and small groups; some churches keep lists of members to call or visit regularly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a throwing word, and Hannah eating her dinner before anything had changed. Your line was he cares for you.

Early in Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, before a single bite of fruit, God looks at something and calls it not good. It isn't a sin. It's a man by himself. "It is not good that the man should be alone." Loneliness is there in the Bible's opening pages, named by God himself as a problem. An apartment where the only voice is the television. A crowded dorm and nobody to call. A kitchen table set for one after years of setting it for two.

You met that verse in year two; now, what the Bible does with it. Psalm 68 says: "God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains." Look who stands next to whom. The solitary, beside the prisoners. The psalm treats loneliness as a kind of captivity, and God as the one who opens the door and walks people into a home. Jesus widens what family means. In Mark, someone tells him his mother and brothers are outside asking for him. He looks at the people sitting around him and says: "Behold my mother and my brethren! For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother." A family you can be set into, not only born into. Then the cross, in John's Gospel. Jesus is dying, and his mother stands there with the disciple he loved. He says to her, "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple, "Behold thy mother!" Then: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." Even then, he makes sure she won't be left alone. Last, the garden. In Gethsemane he asks Peter and two others to stay awake with him, and finds them sleeping: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" So loneliness, in these texts, isn't a failure of faith. Jesus himself asked for company and found his friends asleep. And the setting-in, the psalm's promise, often arrives through a person: someone who calls, who knocks, who takes another person home.

Bring to mind someone who might be lonely right now: a neighbor who lost a spouse, a friend who moved away, a coworker who eats lunch alone, a relative nobody calls much anymore. Let one face come clearly, and if you pray, hold them before God by name. If you're the lonely one and it turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
